units.title: Introduction to Automata Theory
topics: Finite automata as language acceptor and translator
Conversion between Mealy and Moore machines

important_questions.question: Define finite automaton.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton is a mathematical machine with a finite number of states. It reads an input string one symbol at a time and changes state according to its transition function. It accepts a string if it finishes in a final state.

important_questions.question: Differentiate Moore machine and Mealy machine.
important_questions.answer: A Moore machine produces output based only on its present state, whereas a Mealy machine produces output based on its present state and current input. Moore outputs are written on states; Mealy outputs are written on transitions. Mealy machines often need fewer states, while Moore outputs are generally more stable.

important_questions.question: Explain the structure of a finite automaton with a neat diagram.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton consists of a finite set of states (Q), input alphabet (Σ), transition function (δ), start state (q0), and final states (F). It processes each input symbol and moves to the next state. Acceptance occurs when the input is completely read and the current state belongs to F.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
A([Start]) --> B[Read input symbol]
B --> C{Transition function δ}
C --> D[Next state]
D -->|More input| B
D -->|Input finished| E{Final state?}
E -->|Yes| F([Accept])
E -->|No| G([Reject])

important_questions.question: What is the difference between DFA and NFA?
important_questions.answer: In a DFA, for each state and input symbol exactly one next state exists. In an NFA, zero, one or many next states may be possible. Both recognize regular languages.

important_questions.question: What is a regular expression? Give examples.
important_questions.answer: A regular expression is an algebraic notation used to describe a regular language. For alphabet {0,1}, (0+1)* represents all binary strings, including the empty string; 0(0+1)* represents strings beginning with 0.

important_questions.question: Explain the subset construction method for converting NFA into DFA.
important_questions.answer: Start with the set containing the NFA start state (or its epsilon-closure). Treat every set of NFA states as one DFA state. For each input symbol, collect all reachable NFA states and take epsilon-closure if needed. Repeat until no new sets are generated. Any set containing an NFA final state becomes a DFA final state.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([NFA start state]) --> B[Create initial state-set]
B --> C[For each input symbol, find reachable states]
C --> D[Create a new state-set]
D --> E{Any unseen state-set?}
E -->|Yes| C
E -->|No| F[Mark sets containing NFA final state]
F --> G([Equivalent DFA])

important_questions.question: What is a context-free grammar (CFG)?
important_questions.answer: A CFG is a four-tuple G=(V,Σ,P,S), where V is the set of variables, Σ is the set of terminals, P is the set of production rules and S is the start symbol. Each production has one variable on its left side.

important_questions.question: Explain ambiguity in grammar.
important_questions.answer: A grammar is ambiguous if at least one string generated by it has more than one distinct parse tree or more than one leftmost/rightmost derivation. Ambiguity can create multiple interpretations of the same expression.

important_questions.question: Explain Chomsky hierarchy of grammars.
important_questions.answer: The Chomsky hierarchy classifies grammars into four levels: Type-0 unrestricted, Type-1 context-sensitive, Type-2 context-free and Type-3 regular. Their language classes are progressively more restricted: regular is a subset of context-free, which is a subset of context-sensitive, which is a subset of recursively enumerable languages.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TB
A[Type 0: Unrestricted] --> B[Type 1: Context-sensitive]
B --> C[Type 2: Context-free]
C --> D[Type 3: Regular]

important_questions.question: What is a Pushdown Automaton?
important_questions.answer: A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton equipped with a stack. The stack gives it additional memory and enables it to recognize context-free languages.

important_questions.question: Differentiate finite automaton and pushdown automaton.
important_questions.answer: A finite automaton has only finite-state memory and recognizes regular languages. A PDA has an additional stack, can store an unbounded stack sequence, and recognizes context-free languages. Example: a PDA can recognize balanced parentheses.

important_questions.question: Explain the working of a Pushdown Automaton with diagram.
important_questions.answer: A PDA reads an input symbol, checks the top of its stack, changes state and may push or pop stack symbols. Acceptance can be by final state or empty stack, depending on the definition. The stack helps match nested structures such as balanced parentheses.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
A([Input string]) --> B[Finite control]
B <--> C[(Stack memory)]
B --> D{Input consumed and acceptance condition met?}
D -->|Yes| E([Accept])
D -->|No| F([Reject])

units.title: Turing Machine
topics: Multi-tape, multi-head and multidimensional Turing machines

important_questions.question: Define Turing Machine.
important_questions.answer: A Turing Machine is an abstract model of computation consisting of a finite control, an infinite tape and a read/write head. It reads and writes symbols and moves its head left or right according to transition rules.

important_questions.question: Differentiate decidable and undecidable problems.
important_questions.answer: A decidable problem has an algorithm/Turing machine that halts on every input and gives the correct yes/no answer. An undecidable problem has no algorithm that correctly decides every possible input and always halts.

important_questions.question: Explain the Halting Problem and why it is undecidable.
important_questions.answer: The Halting Problem asks whether a given program or Turing Machine eventually stops on a particular input. It is undecidable: assuming a universal algorithm could always answer this question leads to a self-contradiction by constructing a program that does the opposite of the prediction about itself.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([Program + input]) --> B[Hypothetical halting decider]
B --> C{Will it halt?}
C -->|Yes| D[Construct loop forever]
C -->|No| E[Construct halt immediately]
D --> F[Contradiction]
E --> F

units.title: Computer Networks and Layered Architecture
topics: Network definitions, goals, components, architecture, classifications and types
Protocol hierarchy, design issues, interfaces and services
Connection-oriented and connectionless services; service primitives
OSI reference model: layers, principles and comparison with TCP/IP
Physical layer: media, bandwidth, data rate and modulation

important_questions.question: Define a computer network.
important_questions.answer: A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and share data, resources and services through communication links and agreed protocols.

important_questions.question: Differentiate OSI and TCP/IP models.
important_questions.answer: OSI is a 7-layer reference model: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. TCP/IP is the practical Internet protocol suite, commonly represented with 4 layers: Link, Internet, Transport and Application. OSI is a conceptual reference; TCP/IP is widely implemented.

important_questions.question: Explain the OSI reference model with a neat diagram.
important_questions.answer: The OSI model divides communication into seven layers. Each layer provides services to the layer above and uses services from the layer below. The sender encapsulates data while moving downward; the receiver decapsulates it while moving upward.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TB
A[Application] --> B[Presentation]
B --> C[Session]
C --> D[Transport]
D --> E[Network]
E --> F[Data Link]
F --> G[Physical]

units.title: Data Link Layer and Protocols
topics: Data link layer need and services
Framing, flow control and error control
Finite-state machine and Petri-net protocol verification

important_questions.question: What is framing?
important_questions.answer: Framing is the data-link layer process of dividing a continuous bit stream into identifiable units called frames so that the receiver can detect the beginning and end of each data unit.

important_questions.question: Differentiate Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat ARQ.
important_questions.answer: Go-Back-N retransmits the erroneous or lost frame and all subsequent outstanding frames. Selective Repeat retransmits only the specific lost or damaged frames. Selective Repeat is more bandwidth-efficient but requires more buffering and receiver complexity.

important_questions.question: Explain the sliding window protocol.
important_questions.answer: Sliding window is a flow-control and reliability technique. The sender can transmit multiple frames before receiving acknowledgements, up to the window size. As acknowledgements arrive, the window moves forward, allowing new frames to be sent. Sequence numbers identify frames and support retransmission.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
A[Sender window: frames 0,1,2] --> B[Transmit frames]
B --> C[Receiver sends ACK]
C --> D[Window slides forward]
D --> E[Send next frames]

units.title: MAC Sublayer
topics: MAC addressing and Binary Exponential Back-off
Collision-free protocols: Basic Bit Map, BRAP, Binary Countdown and MLMA

important_questions.question: What is CSMA/CD?
important_questions.answer: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection is a medium access method in which a device listens before transmitting and detects collisions while transmitting. On collision, it stops and retries after a back-off time.

important_questions.question: Differentiate Pure ALOHA and Slotted ALOHA.
important_questions.answer: Pure ALOHA allows transmission at any time and has a vulnerable period of two frame times. Slotted ALOHA divides time into slots and permits transmission only at slot boundaries, reducing the vulnerable period to one frame time and improving maximum throughput.

important_questions.question: Explain CSMA/CD with a flow diagram.
important_questions.answer: A station first senses the channel. If busy, it waits. If idle, it transmits and monitors the medium. If a collision is detected, it sends a jam signal, stops transmission, waits for a random back-off interval and tries again.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([Start]) --> B[Sense channel]
B --> C{Channel idle?}
C -->|No| B
C -->|Yes| D[Transmit and monitor]
D --> E{Collision?}
E -->|No| F([Success])
E -->|Yes| G[Jam signal and back-off]
G --> B

units.title: Network Layer
topics: Network layer need, services and design issues
Least-cost routing, Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford algorithms
IP addresses, header format and packet forwarding

important_questions.question: What is an IP address?
important_questions.answer: An IP address is a logical numerical address assigned to a device or network interface so that it can be identified and reached across an IP network.

important_questions.question: Differentiate IPv4 and IPv6.
important_questions.answer: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses written in dotted decimal form, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal groups. IPv6 provides a much larger address space, a simplified base header and improved support for modern network configuration.

important_questions.question: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path routing algorithm.
important_questions.answer: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source node in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Initialize the source distance to zero and all others to infinity. Repeatedly select the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance, relax its outgoing edges, mark it visited and continue until all reachable nodes are processed.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A([Start]) --> B[Set source distance 0; others infinity]
B --> C[Choose unvisited node with minimum distance]
C --> D[Update distances of neighbours]
D --> E[Mark node visited]
E --> F{All reachable nodes visited?}
F -->|No| C
F -->|Yes| G([Shortest paths ready])

units.title: Transport and Application Layers
topics: UDP header and checksum; unicast/multicast real-time traffic
TCP connection management, reliable transfer, flow control and congestion control

important_questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
important_questions.answer: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery using acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless, has lower overhead and does not guarantee delivery or ordering.

important_questions.question: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
important_questions.answer: TCP establishes a connection using three messages: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. After this exchange, both sides can begin data transfer.

important_questions.question: Explain the functions of the application layer and its common protocols.
important_questions.answer: The application layer provides network services directly to user applications. HTTP supports web communication, FTP transfers files, SMTP sends email, IMAP accesses and synchronizes email, DNS maps domain names to IP addresses, SSH provides secure remote login and SNMP monitors network devices.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TB
A[Application Layer] --> B[HTTP: Web]
A --> C[FTP: File transfer]
A --> D[SMTP / IMAP: Email]
A --> E[DNS: Name resolution]
A --> F[SSH: Secure login]
A --> G[SNMP: Monitoring]

units.title: Introduction and Data Communication
topics: Multiplexing: FDM, TDM, WDM and spread spectrum

important_questions.question: What is a computer network?
important_questions.answer: A computer network is a group of interconnected devices that communicate and share data or resources using communication links and agreed protocols.

important_questions.question: Explain the OSI model.
important_questions.answer: The OSI model divides network communication into seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. Each layer performs defined functions and provides services to the layer above it.

important_questions.question: Explain the OSI reference model with a diagram.
important_questions.answer: The OSI model is a seven-layer framework for understanding network communication. Data moves from the Application layer down to Physical layer at the sender, crosses the medium, and moves upward through the layers at the receiver. Each layer communicates logically with its peer layer.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TB
A[Application] --> B[Presentation]
B --> C[Session]
C --> D[Transport]
D --> E[Network]
E --> F[Data Link]
F --> G[Physical]

units.title: Data Link Layer and Medium Access Control
topics: Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat ARQ

important_questions.question: What is CRC?
important_questions.answer: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) is an error-detection technique that treats a bit sequence as a polynomial and uses modulo-2 division to generate a check value.

important_questions.question: Differentiate Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat ARQ.
important_questions.answer: In Go-Back-N, when a frame is lost or damaged, the sender retransmits that frame and all following frames in the window. In Selective Repeat, only the specific lost or damaged frames are retransmitted and correctly received frames can be buffered.

important_questions.question: Explain the working of Stop-and-Wait ARQ.
important_questions.answer: The sender transmits one frame and waits for an acknowledgement. If a valid ACK arrives, it sends the next frame. If the frame or ACK is lost, a timer expires and the sender retransmits the frame. Sequence numbers help identify duplicates.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A[Send one frame] --> B[Start timer and wait for ACK]
B --> C{ACK received?}
C -->|Yes| D[Send next frame]
C -->|No / timeout| E[Retransmit frame]
E --> B

important_questions.question: What is an IP address?
important_questions.answer: An IP address is a logical address assigned to a network interface so that devices can be identified and packets can be routed across IP networks.

important_questions.question: Differentiate IPv4 and IPv6.
important_questions.answer: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses written in dotted-decimal notation, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal groups. IPv6 provides a much larger address space and simplifies several aspects of address configuration and packet handling.

important_questions.question: Explain DHCP operation.
important_questions.answer: A client without an IP address broadcasts a DHCP Discover message. A server responds with an Offer. The client sends a Request for the offered configuration, and the server confirms it with an Acknowledgement. This is commonly called DORA.

units.title: Transport Layer
topics: Leaky Bucket and Token Bucket algorithms

important_questions.question: What is TCP?
important_questions.answer: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgements, sequence numbers and retransmissions.

important_questions.question: Differentiate TCP and UDP.
important_questions.answer: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery with flow and congestion control. UDP is connectionless and has lower overhead but does not guarantee delivery, ordering or retransmission.

important_questions.question: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
important_questions.answer: TCP establishes a connection using three messages. The client sends SYN, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. After these steps, both sides can begin data transfer.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A[Client: SYN] --> B[Server: SYN + ACK]
B --> C[Client: ACK]
C --> D[Connection established]

important_questions.question: What is DNS?
important_questions.answer: The Domain Name System (DNS) translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses and supports other name-related records used by Internet services.

important_questions.question: What is a firewall?
important_questions.answer: A firewall is a hardware or software security control that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic according to defined rules. It helps restrict unauthorized communication.

important_questions.question: Explain how DNS resolves a domain name.
important_questions.answer: A client asks a DNS resolver for a domain's IP address. If the answer is not cached, the resolver queries the DNS hierarchy, obtains the authoritative response, caches it for its TTL and returns the IP address to the client.
important_questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
A[Browser asks for domain] --> B[DNS resolver]
B --> C[DNS hierarchy / authoritative server]
C --> D[IP address returned]
D --> E[Browser connects to server]
